# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXXII. TWO STUBBORN PEOPLE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Clementine Ainslie, while returning to her house after a music lesson at Hollowmere, veered off toward the concealed spring located in Fern Hollow. All summer long, she had avoided the place; that lovely small area had lost its charm for her. Nowadays, her young lover's spirit failed to appear at the meeting place; furthermore, the recollections associated with John Ashdown proved excessively painful and sharp. However, having chanced to look back up the valley, she had observed Lionel Fairlie leaping as lightly as a youth over the ancient stone dyke belonging to the Bailey garden, which made her think he was heading up the hill. Had he caught up to her, she would have been forced to accompany him home, an outcome she intended to avoid. Consequently, she ducked immediately behind the spring's maple trees, wishing he had failed to spot her and would continue past.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0000 }

However, Lionel had spotted her, and beyond that, he was giving chase to her. For a while now, he had desired to converse with Clementine, yet it appeared that she had consistently evaded him. At no point had Clementine ever particularly cared for Lionel Fairlie. She had perpetually been repelled by his bluster, his temper, and his loud merriment. A long time back, she had frequently questioned how Harriet could conceivably find him appealing. Lionel Fairlie was fully conscious of her antipathy, and he laughed softly about it. People disliking Lionel never bothered him. It failed to even render him averse to them in response, because he viewed it as a sort of compelled tribute. He considered Clementine a splendid girl, and he intended to prove himself a superb, open-handed brother-in-law to her. Yet prior to becoming her brother-in-law, a conversation with her was necessary, so, upon catching sight of her departing Hollowmere while he remained in the entrance of a Glen shop, he had immediately charged into the valley to catch up to her.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0001 }

Clementine was seated in a pensive mood on the maple bench that John Ashdown had occupied on that night almost twelve months prior. Underneath its border of ferns, the miniature spring glistened and rippled. Sunlight at dusk cast opal-red glints through the overhanging branches. Beside her blossomed a tall cluster of flawless asters. The small location was just as dreamlike, enchanting, and elusive as any sanctuary of fairies and dryads within primeval woods. Lionel Fairlie burst into this setting, instantly dispersing and destroying its magic. The environment appeared to be completely consumed by his presence. Nothing remained there except Lionel Fairlie, large, red-bearded, and self-satisfied.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0002 }

“Good evening,” Clementine said in a cold tone as she rose to her feet.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0003 }

“‘Good evening, girl. Take a seat once more—take a seat once more. It is my desire to speak with you. Bless the girl, why is she staring at me in that manner? I am not going to devour you—my supper has already been eaten. Take a seat and act politely.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0004 }

“From where I am, I can listen to what you need to tell me just as clearly,” Clementine remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0005 }

“Indeed you are able to, girl, provided you employ your hearing. My sole intention was for you to feel at ease. You appear so blame uncomfortable, remaining on your feet like that. Oh well, I shall take a seat regardless.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0006 }

Lionel therefore took a seat in the exact spot previously occupied by John Ashdown. Clementine feared she might burst into a fit of hysterical laughter because the comparison was so absurd. Throwing his hat to one side, Lionel rested his enormous, red hands upon his knees and peered at her with twinkling eyes.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0007 }

“Don’t act so rigid, girl, come on,” he urged in an attempt to win me over. He possessed a great capacity to be charming whenever he chose to. “Let us engage in a friendly, sensible, and reasonable conversation. I need to inquire about a certain matter. Because Harriet refuses, the responsibility falls on me to ask.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0008 }

Clementine peered below toward the spring, a feature that appeared to have diminished until it was merely as large as a drop of dew. Lionel looked upon her, filled with hopelessness.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0009 }

“Durn it all, you could assist a guy a little,” he suddenly exclaimed.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0010 }

“What do you need my assistance to state?” Clementine inquired with disdain.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0011 }

“Young woman, you are just as aware of this as I am. Stop behaving so dramatically. It is no surprise that Harriet was frightened to make her request to you. Pay attention, girl, Harriet and I intend to get married. Is that not clear enough language? Do you understand? Moreover, Harriet claims she is unable to do so unless you release her from a ridiculous vow she gave you. Now then, are you willing to do it? Are you willing to do it?”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0012 }

“Yes,” Clementine said.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0013 }

Lionel sprang upward and took hold of her unyielding hand.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0014 }

“Good! I was certain you would—I mentioned to Harriet you would. I was aware it would require merely a minute. Now, girl, you head home and inform Harriet, and a fortnight from now we’ll hold a wedding and you’ll reside with us. We will not abandon you to perch on that hill-top such as a solitary crow—do not fret. I am aware you despise me, but, Lord, residing with somebody who despises me will be immense fun. Life will possess some flavor following this. Harriet is going to roast me and you are going to freeze me. A dull moment will not be had by me.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0015 }

Clementine refused to demean herself by informing him that no circumstance could force her to reside in his home. Letting him stride back toward the Glen, radiating happiness and self-satisfaction, she proceeded to walk leisurely up the hill toward her house. Ever since coming back from Portmaris and discovering that Lionel Fairlie had become a regular night visitor, she had anticipated this moment. Although she and Harriet never spoke his name, that deliberate silence spoke volumes. If Clementine had possessed a bitter temperament, she would have experienced great bitterness, but such feelings were foreign to her nature. She maintained a distant politeness toward Lionel, while treating Harriet precisely as she always had. Harriet, however, derived little joy from being courted a second time.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0016 }

Clementine arrived back to find her in the garden, accompanied by St. Laurence. In the dahlia walk, the two sisters came together. St. Laurence positioned himself on the gravel path in their midst, neatly curling his shiny black tail around his white paws, displaying the total nonchalance of a cat that was properly fed, well-bred, and impeccably groomed.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0017 }

“Have you ever laid eyes on such dahlias?” Harriet asked with pride. “They are easily the best we’ve ever grown.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0018 }

Dahlias had never been to Clementine's liking. It was purely to accommodate Harriet’s preference that she allowed them in the garden. Among them, a single gigantic, speckled blossom of red and yellow caught her eye as it dominated the rest.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0019 }

“That dahlia,” she remarked, as she gestured toward it, “is the spitting image of Lionel Fairlie. It could seamlessly pass for his twin brother.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0020 }

Harriet’s sullen face grew red. While she held the dahlia in high regard, she was aware that Clementine held no such affection for it, meaning no praise was meant. Yet she lacked the courage to take offense at Clementine’s remark—the unfortunate Harriet lacked the courage to take offense at anything at that moment. Furthermore, Clementine had never brought up Lionel’s name to her before this moment. It struck her that this boded something.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0021 }

“In the valley, I encountered Lionel Fairlie,” Clementine said, gazing directly toward her sister, “and he informed me that the two of you wished to wed—provided I granted you my consent.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0022 }

“Yes? What did you say?” Harriet inquired, attempting to sound casual and unconcerned, though she failed entirely. Clementine’s gaze was something she was unable to meet. Her eyes dropped to St. Laurence’s smooth back, and an overwhelming fear seized her. Clementine’s statement had been either an agreement or a refusal. Should it be an agreement, Harriet’s shame and regret would render her an exceedingly uneasy bride-to-be; yet should it be a refusal—well, living without Lionel Fairlie was something Harriet had managed in the past, but having forgotten how, she believed the lesson could not be mastered a second time.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0023 }

“I mentioned that, as long as it depended on me, you had complete freedom to wed one another whenever you wished,” Clementine stated.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0024 }

“I am grateful,” Harriet stated, her eyes remaining fixed on St. Laurence.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0025 }

The expression on Clementine’s face grew gentler.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0026 }

“I wish you happiness, Harriet,” she spoke with gentleness.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0027 }

“Oh, Clementine,” Harriet raised her eyes in anguish, “I feel such shame—I am not worthy of it—following everything I told you—”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0028 }

“That is a subject we will not discuss,” Clementine stated with haste and firmness.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0029 }

“Yet—yet,” Harriet kept on, “you are likewise unbound at present—and there is still time—John Ashdown—”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0030 }

“Harriet Ainslie!” Underneath all her sweetness, Clementine possessed a small spark of temper, and right now it flared out from her blue eyes. “Are you completely out of your mind in all regards? Do you imagine even for a moment that I will approach John Ashdown and say submissively, ‘Please, sir, I’ve changed my mind and please, sir, I hope you haven’t changed yours.’ Do you wish for me to do that?”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0031 }

“No—no—but with just a bit of—encouragement—he’d return—”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0032 }

“At no time. He holds me in contempt—and with good reason. Say nothing further about it, Harriet. I hold no resentment toward you—choose anyone you wish for a husband. However, do not interfere with my business.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0033 }

“You have to come live at my place then,” Harriet stated. “Leaving you here by yourself is not something I will do.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0034 }

“Is it your honest belief that I would take up residence in the home of Lionel Fairlie?”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0035 }

“For what reason?” Harriet exclaimed, her humiliation notwithstanding, with a touch of anger.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0036 }

Clementine started laughing.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0037 }

“Harriet, I believed you possessed a sense of humour. Do you picture me performing it?”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0038 }

“I do not understand what would stop you. The size of his house is sufficient—you would possess your own portion of it—he would not intrude.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0039 }

“Harriet, it cannot be considered at all. Do not mention it another time.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0040 }

“In that case,” Harriet stated with a cold, resolute tone, “he and I will not be wed. I refuse to abandon you in this place by yourself. The matter is completely settled.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0041 }

“Nonsense, Harriet.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0042 }

“This isn't foolishness. My mind is completely made up. You contemplating residing in this place alone—a mile away from all other homes—would be ridiculous. Should you refuse to accompany me, I am going to remain with you. At this point, we will not debate the issue, so do not attempt to.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0043 }

“I will permit Lionel to handle the debate,” Clementine remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0044 }

“Lionel will be handled by me, as I am capable of managing him. Never would I have requested the return of my promise from you—not ever—yet the reason I was unable to wed Lionel had to be explained to him, and he stated his intention to ask you himself. Stopping him was beyond my power. It is unnecessary for you to assume that self-respect belongs solely to you in this world. The idea of getting married and deserting you here by yourself never entered my mind. Furthermore, you will discover that my determination equals your own.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0045 }

Shrugging her shoulders, Clementine turned around and walked into the dwelling. Harriet glanced toward St. Laurence, who had not moved a whisker or blinked an eyelash throughout the entire encounter.
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0046 }

“St. Laurence, I’ll grant that this world would be dreary lacking the men, yet I am nearly inclined to desire that not a single one of ‘em existed in it. See the difficulty and fuss they have caused in this very place, Laurence—utterly uprooted our joyful former life, Saint. John Ashdown started it and Lionel Fairlie has completed it. And at present each of them must depart into limbo. Lionel stands as the sole man I have ever encountered who concurs with me that the Kaiser of Germany is the most perilous being living upon this earth—and I am unable to wed this reasonable individual because my sister is unyielding and I am more unyielding. Take note of what I say, St. Laurence, the minister would return if she lifted her pinky. However she will not Laurence—she will under no circumstances do so—she will not so much as bend it—and I dare not interfere, Saint. I shall not brood, Laurence; Clementine refrained from brooding, therefore I am set on not doing so either, Saint; Lionel will throw a fury, yet the bottom line is, St. Laurence, that every one of us aged fools has to simply cease contemplating marriage. Ah well, ‘despair is a free man, hope is a slave,’ Saint. Therefore come inside the house now, Laurence, and I will comfort you using a small bowl filled with cream. At that point there shall be at least one joyful and satisfied being upon this hill.”
{: #nw-v05-c32-p0047 }
